{{Short description|Graph whose edges are given independent directions at both ends}}
[[File:Bidirected graph features.svg|thumb|360px|The different types of edge in a bidirected graph]]

In the [[mathematics|mathematical]] domain of [[graph theory]], a '''bidirected graph''' (introduced by {{harvnb|Edmonds|Johnson|1970}})<ref>{{citation
 | last1 = Edmonds | first1 = Jack | authorlink1 = Jack Edmonds
 | last2 = Johnson | first2 = Ellis L.
 | contribution = Matching: a well-solved class of linear programs
 | title = Combinatorial Structures and their Applications: Proceedings of the Calgary Symposium, June 1969
 | publisher = Gordon and Breach | location = New York | year = 1970 
}}. Reprinted in ''Combinatorial Optimization — Eureka, You Shrink!'', Springer-Verlag, Lecture Notes in Computer Science 2570, 2003, pp. 27–30, {{doi|10.1007/3-540-36478-1_3}}.
</ref> is a [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] in which each [[Edge (graph theory)|edge]] is given an independent [[Orientation (graph theory)|orientation]] (or direction, or arrow) at each end. 

There are three kinds of bidirected edges: '''''extraverted''''', where the arrows point outward, towards the [[Vertex (graph theory)|vertices]], at both ends; '''''introverted''''', where both arrows point inward, away from the vertices; and '''''directed''''', in which the two arrows have the same direction (one arrow points away from its vertex and towards the opposite end, while the other arrow points in the same direction as the first, away from the opposite end and towards its own vertex). The bidirected edges of kind ''directed'' are the same as ordinary directed edges in a [[directed graph]]; thus, a directed graph is a special kind of bidirected graph.

It is sometimes desirable to have also edges with only one end ('''half-edges'''); these get only one arrow.  An edge with no ends (a '''loose edge''') has no arrows.  The edges that are neither half nor loose edges may be called '''ordinary edges'''.

A [[skew-symmetric graph]] is the [[Bipartite double cover|double covering graph]] of a bidirected graph.

A bidirected graph may be regarded as an orientation of a [[signed graph]], similarly to how a directed graph may be viewed as an orientation of an ordinary [[undirected graph]].

==Other meanings==

A symmetric [[directed graph]] (that is, a directed graph in which the reverse of every edge is also an edge) is sometimes also called a "bidirected graph".<ref name="MehlhornSanders2008">{{citation
 | last1 = Mehlhorn | first1 = Kurt | author1-link = Kurt Mehlhorn
 | last2 = Sanders | first2 = Peter | author2-link = Peter Sanders (computer scientist)
 | isbn = 978-3-540-77978-0
 | pages = 49 and 170–171
 | publisher = Springer Science & Business Media
 | title = Algorithms and Data Structures: The Basic Toolbox
 | url = https://people.mpi-inf.mpg.de/~mehlhorn/ftp/Toolbox/
 | year = 2008}}</ref>
